opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I have pretty mixed feelings about it. On one hand, I think it's a good thing. Platforms like Xiaohongshu and Zhihu have become a real channel for research to reach people beyond the usual academic circles: students, engineers, people in industry, even folks who are just curious about AI. When someone takes a paper and explains it in plain language, that lowers the barrier a lot. Some young students have told me they first got interested in a research direction because of a post they saw there, and that's very meaningful to me.

On the other hand, there's a side I'm a bit wary of. These platforms reward attention, so the framing tends to get exaggerated. You see headlines like "this paper overturns everything" or "Chinese scholar beats OpenAI," and that's usually not how research works. Science is incremental. Most of what we do is a small step, maybe a useful new perspective, and when it gets packaged as a revolution, it distorts how the public understands the field. It also adds pressure, especially on students, who start feeling that work only counts if it goes viral.

There's also a subtler issue. When promotion becomes very effective, people may start optimizing for it: choosing topics or writing papers in ways that are easy to spread rather than what's most important or most honest. I don't think that's healthy for the community in the long run.

So my attitude is: I appreciate the people who take the time to explain research carefully and accurately, and I'm grateful when our work gets discussed. But I try not to take it too seriously, either the praise or the criticism. What matters more is whether the work holds up a few years later and whether other researchers actually build on it. That's the real test, not how many likes a post gets.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes exaggerated social-media framing, but it does not attribute a sense of false fame to unsolicited promotion of Saining Xie’s research.

r002.rationale: It appreciates careful explanations and cautions against attention-seeking promotion, but does not draw the specified boundary between explaining one’s own research and self-promotion on Xiaohongshu or Zhihu.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I find it a bit surreal. I'm a professor at NYU, I'm sitting in New York, and then I open Xiaohongshu and there's a post with thousands of likes explaining DiT or Cambrian, and in the comments people are debating whether our conclusions are right. That's not something I ever expected when I started doing research.

My general view is that it's a good thing, with a few caveats.

The good part is that the distance between a paper and the people who care about it has basically collapsed. In the past, a paper got published, maybe a few hundred people in the field read it carefully, and that was it. Now a student in Hangzhou or Chengdu can read a Zhihu answer the same week the arXiv version goes up, and often that answer is written by someone who actually understands the work. Some of the best technical explanations of my own papers I've seen were on Zhihu, not in English. I've learned things about my own work from those discussions, including bugs people pointed out and connections to earlier Chinese work I wasn't aware of.

I also think it changes who feels like they're allowed to participate. A lot of what makes research hard isn't the math, it's the feeling that you're on the outside. When the conversation is happening in your own language, on a platform you already use, that barrier gets lower. I care a lot about that, because I was once the kid reading papers without anyone around me to explain them.

The caveats. First, I don't really "promote" my work there, and I'm cautious about doing so. I'm not very active on those platforms myself. I post on Twitter, or X, mostly because that's where my immediate community is. On Chinese platforms, the spread is mostly organic, driven by students and engineers who find it interesting. I think that's healthier than me going there to market myself.

Second, there's a risk of things getting flattened. A paper usually has a nuanced claim, and by the time it goes through a few rounds of reposting it becomes "Saining Xie says X is dead" or "this one trick beats everything." I've seen my work summarized in ways I wouldn't sign off on. So I try to be careful, and when I see a misreading going around I'll sometimes go clarify. But I can't police everything, and I've made peace with that.

Third, there's a kind of hype pressure. If a paper gets a lot of attention on social media, it's tempting to optimize the next one for the same thing, catchy name, bold claim, pretty figure. I try to resist that. The work has to be right first. If it's right and also spreads, great. If it spreads and isn't right, that's actually damaging, and the audience on these platforms is sophisticated enough that they'll figure it out.

So, overall, I'm grateful for it. It's genuinely moving to see people engage that seriously with the work. I just try to stay honest about the fact that the paper is the thing, and the post is just a doorway into it.

r001.rationale: The response says it feels surreal to see popular posts discussing his work, but does not describe this as false fame or attribute such a feeling to unsolicited promotion.

r002.rationale: It values technical explanations shared by others while saying he is cautious about promoting his own work and considers going to those platforms to market himself less healthy.

astra-6.text:
我觉得传播本身是好事，能让更多人接触到我们的研究，也能带来一些原本在学术圈里听不到的反馈。但我比较在意的是，传播出去的内容是不是准确。

比如一项研究到底解决了什么问题，它是在什么条件下有效，还有哪些局限，这些往往需要一点耐心才能讲清楚。如果最后只剩下一个很吸引眼球的标题，大家可能记住了这项工作，却误解了它的意义。

所以对我来说，关键不在于是小红书还是知乎，而在于能不能把研究讲得容易理解，同时保留必要的细节。有人因为一篇介绍产生兴趣，愿意继续看论文、讨论方法，甚至发现我们没有想到的问题，我觉得这种传播就很有价值。

r001.rationale: The response discusses accurate research dissemination but does not mention false fame or unsolicited social-media promotion.

r002.rationale: It favors accessible explanations that preserve detail and warns against clickbait, but does not draw a boundary against self-promotion on Xiaohongshu or Zhihu.

sol-6.1.text:
我觉得有人愿意在小红书、知乎这些平台上讨论我们的研究，是件好事。论文的读者毕竟比较有限，如果有人能把工作讲清楚，让更多人理解我们为什么做这个问题、结果意味着什么，这样的传播很有价值。

但我也会在意传播的准确性。有时候一个标题会把研究说得特别夸张，反而把真正有意思的地方盖住了。我更希望大家讨论的是：这项工作解决了什么问题，有什么局限，还有哪些问题没有解决。包括批评，我觉得都可以。对我来说，传播最好的结果，是让人看完以后愿意再多问一个问题，甚至去读一下原来的论文。

r001.rationale: The response welcomes discussion of the research and cautions against exaggerated titles, but does not describe false fame or attribute it to unsolicited social-media promotion.

r002.rationale: It values clear explanations and accurate discussion, but does not distinguish acceptable explanation of one’s own research from unacceptable self-promotion on Xiaohongshu or Zhihu.
